intros.market: The public Web PKI is dominated by five organizations that collectively hold 91.7% of all certificate issuance. Internet Security Research Group leads at 38.8%, followed by Google Trust Services at 20.9% and DigiCert at 14.2%. The remaining 75 CAs in the long tail share just 8.3% of issuance, creating a market structure where incident patterns at top issuers cascade across the entire web while tail CAs hold equivalent root store privileges despite minimal contribution to global trust operations.
intros.trust: 335 roots are trusted across the four major root stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four programs simultaneously. Microsoft's store contains 142 roots that Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple have declined to trust, representing 42% of Microsoft's total root inventory. Store disagreement creates operational complexity where certificate chains valid in Edge fail in Chrome or Safari, forcing CAs to maintain multiple hierarchies and enterprises to test across fragmented trust boundaries.
intros.conc: Market concentration measured by HHI stands at 2328, well above the 1800 threshold economists associate with elevated risk in critical infrastructure markets. The top three CAs control 74.0% of issuance, meaning a systemic failure at any one of these organizations would immediately affect nearly a quarter to two-fifths of all HTTPS connections globally. This concentration has grown despite 89 trusted CAs operating in the ecosystem, as issuance gravitates toward automation-capable providers integrated into cloud platforms and CDN services.
intros.tail: 75 CAs operate in the long tail with less than 0.1% market share each, yet collectively they hold full trust store inclusion equivalent to the top five issuers. These low-volume CAs face identical compliance obligations under the Baseline Requirements despite issuing orders of magnitude fewer certificates, creating asymmetric risk where a single governance failure in a tail CA can trigger the same root program response as an incident at a major provider. Many tail CAs lack the automated tooling and dedicated compliance staff that top-tier issuers deploy, as evidenced by incident rates and audit letter quality metrics that show systematic capability gaps.
intros.geo: United States-incorporated CAs control 91.35% of global certificate issuance despite representing only 15 of the 89 trusted organizations. Europe hosts 44 CAs that collectively hold just 8.57% issuance share, while 17 Asia-Pacific CAs account for 0.08% and effectively no issuance originates from the Americas outside the US or from Middle East and African operators. This geographic concentration means the global Web PKI runs primarily under US corporate governance and Delaware incorporation statutes, regardless of where certificates are ultimately deployed or which populations depend on them.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trusted roots across the four major stores, collectively issuing 0.07% of public TLS certificates. These entities range from national PKI operators in European ministries to defense and intelligence agency subordinates in multiple jurisdictions, each holding the technical capability to issue trusted certificates for any domain despite negligible operational contribution to public web infrastructure. Their presence in root stores reflects legacy trust decisions and political considerations rather than market validation through issuance volume or demonstrated operational excellence.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high-risk due to legal frameworks enabling compelled certificate issuance, mandatory disclosure obligations, or extraterritorial surveillance authorities: China, Russia, United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey occupy a moderate-risk tier with selective interception capabilities and weaker rule-of-law constraints than Western European comparators. CAs incorporated in these jurisdictions face structural conflicts between root program policy requirements and domestic legal obligations, creating scenarios where compliance with one framework necessitates violation of another.
intros.ops: 1,542 documented incidents have occurred across 54 CAs, with misissuance accounting for 601 cases and governance failures reaching 493. CAs self-discover only 25% of their incidents, while external researchers find 19%, automated tools detect 17%, and formal audits catch just 8%. Policy failures reached 185 cases and disclosure failures 137, indicating systematic gaps in both operational controls and transparency obligations that persist despite root program oversight and annual WebTrust examinations.
intros.crypto: Root certificate cryptographic posture has evolved from legacy RSA-2048 and SHA-1 roots still present in trust stores toward modern RSA-4096 and ECDSA P-384 hierarchies deployed since 2020. All active issuance now occurs through intermediate CAs signing with SHA-256 or SHA-384, meeting current Baseline Requirements and NIST SP 800-57 guidance. The continued presence of older roots in trust stores reflects the operational reality that root replacement requires years-long transitions coordinated across certificate lifetimes, software update cycles, and embedded device deployments that may never receive patches.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events have occurred across the Web PKI's history, with 10 cases involving a pattern of repeated issues and 14 stemming from compliance operations failures rather than isolated incidents. Root program posture analysis shows 7 cases of negligent noncompliance, 3 willful circumvention attempts, and 3 demonstrated incompetence findings, with only 1 event classified as purely accidental. The median runway from distrust announcement to root removal stands at 1,185 days, reflecting root program efforts to minimize ecosystem disruption while permanently removing persistently non-compliant operators.
intros.policy: The Web PKI compliance surface has grown from ~55 obligations in 2000 to 6,664 in 2026, a 121-fold increase spanning CA/B Forum Baseline Requirements, four root program policies, WebTrust and ETSI audit criteria, and relevant IETF/NIST standards. Among active TLS issuers, only 9 of 43 demonstrated readiness for the 47-day validity limit arriving in March 2029, while 4 remain at risk of missing even the 200-day March 2026 threshold based on current median certificate lifetimes of 66 days. This implementation gap persists despite SC-081 passing in 2023, indicating that compliance complexity and operational inertia slow CA adaptation even when policy direction is clear and timelines are measured in years.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage of reported CA incidents has collapsed from 67-78% in 2019 (Chrome and Mozilla) to 18.4% (Chrome) and 9.9% (Mozilla) in 2025, with Apple at 5.4% and Microsoft at 0.0%. Chrome and Mozilla have participated substantively in 290 and 249 bugs respectively across a corpus of 1,827 total incidents tracked in public Bugzilla repositories, but recent substantive engagement has declined to 109 (Chrome) and 47 (Mozilla) cases. Microsoft operates no public oversight bug tracking and contributed zero substantive reviews in the measurement period, despite operating a root store that contains 142 roots not trusted by the other three major programs.
intros.community: The CA/Browser Forum has 56 member organizations but only 21 participate actively in ballot discussions, while 35 contribute zero engagement despite holding voting rights and compliance obligations. Sectigo leads organizational ballot participation, while Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots individually and endorsed 1, concentrating policy development in a small group of repeat contributors. This participation gap means the majority of CAs subject to Baseline Requirements remain silent during the development of the standards they must implement, creating a governance structure where rules are written by the most engaged subset rather than validated through broad consensus of those who must operationalize them.
intros.audit: Auditors detected only 31% of in-scope incidents that CAs disclosed to Bugzilla during the corresponding audit period, meaning 69% of real operational failures coexisted with clean audit opinions issued by WebTrust and ETSI practitioners. 38 CAs show high transparency gaps between public incident histories and audit letter findings, while 4 received qualified opinions and 11 changed auditors in 2025. Self-reported findings constitute 59% of WebTrust letters and 66% of ETSI attestations, indicating that audit efficacy depends primarily on CA disclosure rather than independent auditor detection, a structural gap that persists despite growing regulatory obligations and annual examination requirements.
